answer: FINAL HYPOTHESIS: The variable is **SES (socioeconomic status)**. In a baseline logistic regression predicting BA degree completion, SES has a positive coefficient (≈0.35–0.36 in standardized units; 0.3511 in our refit, matching the quoted 0.3636 within ~3%). Once race (Black/Hispanic dummies, White reference) and academic characteristics (ASVAB ability composite + percentile in class) are included as controls, the SES coefficient drops to ≈ −0.23 (−0.2316 in our raw-scale refit vs. the quoted −0.2293) and loses practical significance. This sign reversal is the fingerprint of confounding/omitted-variable bias: SES is strongly correlated with both race (mean SES: White +0.18, Black −0.21, Hispanic −0.45) and academic performance (r = 0.46 with the ability composite, r = 0.30 with class percentile), and BA completion rates differ sharply by race (White 3.5% vs. Black/Hispanic ~1.3–1.4%). The baseline positive SES "effect" was therefore largely carried by these correlated factors; conditioning on them leaves no meaningful independent positive effect of SES. No other variable shows this pattern: ABILITY stays positive and highly significant (0.0037 → 0.0029), PERCENTILE stays positive (0.0450 → 0.0218), FAMILY SIZE stays negative (−0.508 → −0.525), and Male is insignificant in both models.

payload.hypothesis: SES (socioeconomic status): its coefficient on BA degree completion falls from ~0.36 (baseline logistic model, ≈0.3511 in refit) to ~−0.23 (full model with race dummies + ASVAB ability composite + class percentile; −0.2316 in refit) and becomes insignificant, because SES is a confounder correlated with both race (SES means: White +0.18, Black −0.21, Hispanic −0.45) and academic performance (r=0.46 with ability, r=0.30 with class percentile); controlling for these factors leaves no independent positive effect of SES on BA completion.
payload.workflow: Loaded and validated nls_ses_processed.csv (8,773 rows, 0 missing, 3 race categories, binary outcome at 2.7%). Fitted univariate logistic regressions of BA_DEGREE_COMPLETED on each candidate predictor (raw and z-standardized). Fitted the full logistic model BA ~ SES + Black + Hispanic + ABILITY composite + PERCENTILE IN CLASS in raw and standardized variants; grid-searched 24+ specification variants (±sex, ±family size, 3-dummy coding, robust HC0-HC3 SEs) to locate the quoted 0.3636 -> -0.2293 transition. Tested significance via Wald z-test (p<0.05), ran an OLS linear-probability sensitivity check, and verified collinearity (VIF <= 2.6). SES was the only variable whose coefficient reversed from positive to negative upon adding race and academic controls, confirming it as the answer; attenuation attributed to confounding between SES, race, and academic performance.
